pharm: Mandelic acid ester with direct relaxant (papaverine-like) action on vascular smooth muscle, formerly used to improve peripheral and cerebral blood flow; efficacy is unproven.
quick: Historical: 1.2-1.6 g/day in divided doses (largely obsolete)
Take with food/milk to reduce GI upset
summary: Cyclandelate is a direct-acting peripheral vasodilator and smooth-muscle relaxant that was historically used for peripheral and cerebral vascular disorders (e.g., intermittent claudication, Raynaud's phenomenon, nocturnal leg cramps, age-related cognitive/cerebrovascular complaints). It relaxes vascular smooth muscle independently of autonomic innervation. It is not FDA-approved, its clinical efficacy was never convincingly demonstrated, and it is now largely obsolete and withdrawn from most markets. Typical historical oral dosing was 1.2-1.6 g/day in divided doses.
indications: Historical: peripheral vascular disease / intermittent claudication
Historical: Raynaud's phenomenon and other peripheral vasospastic disorders
Historical: cerebrovascular insufficiency and associated cognitive/behavioral symptoms in the elderly
Note: all uses are of unproven efficacy; the drug is largely withdrawn/obsolete

dosage.n: Typical historical maintenance range; taken with meals to limit GI upset

admin: Was taken orally in divided doses with food or milk to minimize gastrointestinal irritation
Onset of any clinical effect was gradual; a trial of several weeks was historically suggested
Dose was tapered to the lowest effective maintenance level after initial response

moa: Direct, papaverine-like relaxant action on vascular smooth muscle, producing vasodilation independent of autonomic nerve supply (possibly via interference with smooth-muscle calcium utilization / phosphodiesterase-type activity). The intended effect was increased peripheral and cerebral blood flow, but a meaningful clinical benefit was never established.

relative: Severe obliterative coronary artery or cerebrovascular disease (vasodilation may divert flow / 'steal')

preg: Avoid; safety in pregnancy not established.
lact: Avoid; no data on excretion in breast milk.
renal: No established dose adjustment; use with general caution.
hepatic: No established dose adjustment; use with caution in hepatic impairment.

moderate: Antihypertensives and other vasodilators - additive hypotensive effect
minor: Other agents causing flushing or dizziness
interactions.food: Take with food or milk to reduce gastrointestinal upset; no major food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: May potentiate vasodilation, flushing and hypotension; use caution.

rare: Worsening of angina or 'steal' in severe vascular disease

monitoring: Symptoms of flushing, headache, or dizziness
Clinical response - recognizing that efficacy is unproven
counsel: This medicine is outdated, not FDA-approved, and was never proven to work - discuss alternatives with your clinician
Flushing, headache, dizziness, and tingling can occur, especially early in treatment and usually lessen over time
Take with food or milk to reduce stomach upset
Rise slowly from sitting or lying to avoid light-headedness
Avoid or limit alcohol, which can worsen flushing and low blood pressure
pk: Gradual; any clinical effect develops over days to weeks
Oral absorption with peak within a few hours (limited data)
Short; not well characterized in the literature
Store at controlled room temperature in a dry place (historical product)
pearls: Not FDA-approved and of unproven efficacy - controlled trials failed to demonstrate meaningful benefit, and the drug is now largely withdrawn/obsolete
One of several older 'cerebral/peripheral vasodilators' (with isoxsuprine, naftidrofuryl, cinnarizine) whose clinical value was never established
Theoretical risk of vascular 'steal' in severe obstructive disease - dilating healthy vessels may divert flow away from ischemic tissue

Where peripheral arterial disease is genuinely present, evidence-based measures (risk-factor control, exercise, antiplatelet therapy, and agents such as cilostazol or naftidrofoxen per local guidance) are preferred
Effects are largely limited to flushing, headache and dizziness; serious toxicity is uncommon
missed: Not clinically relevant as the drug is obsolete. (Historically: take the missed dose when remembered, skip it if near the next scheduled dose, and do not double up.)
overdose: Limited data; overdose would be expected to cause exaggerated vasodilatory effects - marked flushing, headache, dizziness, tachycardia and hypotension. Management is supportive: place the patient supine, give IV fluids for hypotension, monitor vital signs, and provide symptomatic care. No specific antidote.
